app: Quarto — essays and archive writing (untouched case U2: editorial long-form)
subtitle: Essays on archives, cities and the paper that outlives us.

records.title: Box fourteen
records.author: Ananya Iyer
records.standfirst: A box nobody had opened in thirty years turned out to be the only complete record of a demolished neighbourhood.
body: The archive was never meant to be read. It was meant to be kept.
Then a researcher requested box fourteen, and the request went through four desks before anyone could say whether the box still existed.
What follows is an account of eleven weeks, three storage units and one very patient archivist.

records.title: The room where the paper goes
records.author: Rehan Mirza
records.standfirst: Every city keeps one. Most are closing.
body: Every city has a room where the paper goes.
Usually it is a basement, usually it smells of dust and mild regret, and usually the person who runs it has been there longer than the building's current name.
This is a piece about those rooms, and about what happens when they close.

records.title: Reading only old sentences
records.author: Ananya Iyer
records.standfirst: A month with nothing published after 1970.
body: I spent a month reading only things printed before 1970.
It is a strange discipline. The sentences are longer, the assumptions are louder, and the confidence is total in a way that reads now as almost charming.
The point was not nostalgia. It was to notice what current prose takes for granted.

records.title: A map wrong for sixty years
records.author: Meghna Das
records.standfirst: The bridge was gone. The road was never there. Nobody minded.
body: The map was wrong for sixty years and nobody minded.
It showed a bridge that had been demolished in 1954 and omitted a road that carries eleven thousand vehicles a day.
Both facts were known. Neither was urgent.

records.title: Notes toward a theory of the photocopy
records.author: Rehan Mirza
records.standfirst: An argument about what deserves to exist twice.
body: Notes toward a theory of the photocopy.
A photocopy is an argument about what matters: someone decided this page, not that one, deserved to exist twice.
That decision is usually invisible, and it is the most interesting thing about the object.
